📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Matt Law | 27 Nov 2026 14:31, Last updated: 27 Nov 2026 14:32.

Manchester United have reportedly activated an option to extend the contract of captain Bruno Fernandes until the summer of 2028.

Fernandes' current deal had been due to expire at the end of the 2026-27 campaign, meaning that foreign clubs would have been free to agree a contract with the Portugal international in January.

Man United are working to sign their captain to a new long-term deal, but discussions have been placed on hold amid the team's struggles.

Fernandes noted ahead of Wednesday's Champions League clash with Sporting Lisbon that his current focus was on helping the club navigate their way through an incredibly difficult period.

"For us to start winning games and then we can talk about contract," Fernandes told reporters when asked what would need to happen for him to sign a new deal.

It has been revealed that "It’s not vital now. It’s my future, I haven’t got much left in my contract, but we will have time to speak about that. The conversations stopped when we thought now was not the moment.".

However, according to The Athletic, Man United have now activated their one-year option, meaning that the attacker's deal now runs until the summer of 2028.

An excellent 2025-26 campaign saw Fernandes earn the FWA Footballer of the Year and PFA Player of the Year awards, with the 32-year-old breaking the Premier League assist record to register 21 in a single season.

There has been criticism of the attacker's form this season, but he has still come up with eight goals and three assists in 16 appearances in all competitions.

Fernandes has four goals and two assists in 10 Premier League appearances this season, while he struck twice against Sporting in the Champions League on Wednesday to make it four goals and one assist in five appearances in the competition this term.

The Red Devils captain had been in line to make his 11th Premier League appearance of the season against Brentford on Saturday afternoon, but he has now emerged as a major doubt for that match due to an illness.

Man United head coach Mauricio Pochettino said during Friday's press conference that a final decision on Fernandes' involvement would not be made until Saturday morning.

There remains speculation surrounding Fernandes' long-term future at Old Trafford, with Man United thought to be putting plans in place in the event that the Portuguese leaves at the end of the season; Como's Nico Paz is said to be a genuine option for the Red Devils.

Fernandes will go down as one of Man United's best-ever signings considering his output, scoring 115 goals and registering 111 assists in 343 appearances for the Red Devils since arriving from Sporting in January 2020.

By Seye Omidiora | 27 Nov 2026 14:44, Last updated: 27 Nov 2026 14:54.

Fresh from their first victory under Thomas Frank on Thursday, Crystal Palace welcome Hull City to Selhurst Park in Sunday's matchweek 13 encounter aiming to end their five-match losing league run.

The bottom-placed Eagles sit nine places below their visitors in the Premier League table but hope to draw inspiration from their Europa League success and collect maximum points in the Dane's first home top-flight fixture.

After conceding a late winner against Coventry City on Frank's managerial debut for Palace last weekend, the capital club enjoyed a change of fortune as Dwight McNeil struck in the 81st minute to secure their second European victory.

The winger's goal sealed Palace's first win since beating Fulham in the EFL Cup a month ago, and they now seek consecutive victories for the first time since overcoming the Cottagers and Middlesbrough in the league and domestic cup respectively in early September.

That ambition will be difficult to realise for the Eagles, whose inability to keep clean sheets continues to undermine them, with Mamadou Sarr's 66th-minute goal marking a fifth consecutive match in which the Londoners have conceded.

Their EFL Cup shutout remains Palace's only clean sheet in 11 matches, underlining their broader problems, particularly when they cannot rely on Jean-Philippe Mateta's usual attacking influence.

It remains to be seen whether Frank can address those weaknesses before Sunday's encounter, as the bottom-placed Eagles pursue their first league victory since early October's 3-1 success over Nottingham Forest in an attempt to escape the relegation zone.

Hull's modest scoring figures may not frighten the division's worst defence, but Sergej Jakirovic will know that Coventry were hardly prolific before scoring three in last weekend's 3-2 victory over Palace to reach 13 league goals.

The Tigers also have 13 goals after 11 matches, exceeding Coventry's tally before last weekend and suggesting that the promoted outfit can threaten the division's leakiest defence.

Last season's Championship playoff winners travel to Selhurst Park buoyed by their victory over Brighton & Hove Albion, secured through two goals in second-half stoppage time to end a three-month wait for maximum points in the competition.

That success lifted Jakirovic's team to 11th in the Premier League table, and consecutive victories for the first time since the opening two gameweeks could propel them into the top half, with their 14 points just three short of sixth-placed Brentford.

Having remained difficult to beat throughout their three-month winless spell, Hull now hope to leave any anxiety behind and find the consistency to demonstrate that they belong at this level.

Crystal Palace Premier League form:.

Crystal Palace form (all competitions):.

Mateta will serve the final game of his suspension this weekend, while Yeremy Pino is also banned after collecting his fifth yellow card of the season in the defeat to Coventry.

With Ismaila Sarr also unavailable due to a groin problem, the Eagles are missing several potential match-winners and will look to McNeil and Jorgen Strand Larsen, who has already registered one goal and two assists under Frank.

Takehiro Tomiyasu (calf) and Chadi Riad (knee) are also sidelined for the hosts on Sunday.

Hull also have several injury concerns: Charlie Hughes will be assessed before the trip to south London, while Hidemasa Morita (muscle), Ilyas Ansah (back), Joe Gelhardt (thigh), Matt Targett (ankle), Eliot Matazo (knee) and Tim Iroegbunam (thigh) are also carrying injuries.

Oli McBurnie and Mohamed Belloumi were instrumental in the Tigers' latest victory, with McBurnie scoring both late goals and Belloumi providing one assist to take their respective goal contributions for the season to six apiece.

Crystal Palace possible starting lineup:.

Henderson; Khalaili, Richards, Disasi, Mitchell; Timber, Wharton; McNeil, Kamada, Guessand; Strand Larsen.

Hull City possible starting lineup:.

Tzolakis; Coyle, Ajayi, Mendy, Stroud; Slater, Gourna-Douath; Belloumi, Crooks, Thomas; McBurnie.

Palace may struggle to build on Thursday's victory without Mateta, Pino and Sarr, particularly with the quick turnaround limiting Frank's preparation time.

Hull remained competitive throughout their prolonged winless spell, and McBurnie's decisive display against Brighton suggests that the visitors could punish another defensive lapse to edge this encounter.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 17:18 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 05:01 EST, 26 November 2026.

A week into the job and Mauricio Pochettino must be getting used to the madness of Manchester United by now.

If it's not drones flying over the training ground, red card controversies and random divots of grass, it's his own players shooting themselves in the foot.

At least, Pochettino emerged from the craziness in Lisbon with a draw on a night when Bruno Fernandes celebrated his return to the Jose Alvalade Stadium with a couple of goals.

But these are the kind of nights that must drive coaches like Pochettino potty. After the carnage of Michael Carrick's final two games in charge against Roma and Aston Villa, and the rancour of the Argentine's introduction to the Old Trafford circus at Anfield on Sunday, this was another mad, mad spectacle.

Where do we start? The two acts of self-sabotage by goalkeeper Senne Lammens? United's two disallowed goals? The first was harsh on the scorer, Amad Diallo, but also Youri Tielemans who received a booking that led to his sending-off in injury-time. Or maybe that divot, which Fernandes claimed he created and then hit to put United ahead with a bizarre deflected goal?

At the end of all the chaos, United had conceded five penalties in their last five games and picked up four red cards.

Senne Lammens (left) two errors cost Man United a deserving win at Sporting as they drew.

New United head coach Mauricio Pochettino comforts Lammens at full-time after his mistakes.

That is not something that will sit well with Pochettino. But after venting his frustration with the officiating over Leny Yoro's sending-off at Anfield, which dominated the build-up to this game after it was rescinded, here was another sequence of events that seemed to conspire against him.

Sources indicate that it's not as if the Jose Alvalade Stadium was a cauldron of emotion to scramble the senses of the two sets of players and match officials either. Fernandes got a polite round of applause from the fans and a framed memento from his old club before kick-off.

When the teams came out, he was one of three former United players alongside Cristiano Ronaldo and Luis Nani honoured on a tifo of the Sporting Lisbon greats.

It was all very flat until the half-hour mark when United self-imploded again. Geny Catamo picked up the ball on the edge of the United box and teased Lisandro Martinez, playing at left back.

United's lead was undone late on when Lammens' second major error allowed Suarez to score.

United's evening was compounded when Tielemans was sent off late on for a second yellow.

Two minutes later, and having made the divot turning in the penalty box 17 seconds earlier, Fernandes somehow managed to hit it with a hopeful effort from 25 yards. Pereira had the ball covered but it took an outrageous deflection just outside the six-yard box and flew through his arms.

According to recent reports, but this is United and nothing is straightforward. Tonda Eckert described his Southampton side's victory over Middlesbrough as "one of the best games the Championship could produce".

It has been revealed that the Saints won 2-0 at St. Mary's Stadium after second-half goals from Ryan Manning and Finn Azaz, with the latter running the full length of the pitch to celebrate in front of the away end against his former side.

Much of the build-up to the match was focused on the 'Spygate' scandal from the end of last season, but Southampton managed to put that to one side on Friday to move within four points of Championship leaders Boro.

Boro had their chances, accumulating 1.4 expected goals (xG) from 19 shots to Southampton's 1.12 from 12 attempts, but Kim Hellberg's side went scoreless again on the road.

They have failed to score in three consecutive Championship away games for the first time since January 2015, having 49 shots without success.

The Saints, meanwhile, extended their unbeaten run at home to 19 games in the league (W15 D4), and Eckert was delighted with the result.

"I think [that was] one of the best games the Championship could produce," Eckert told Sky Sports.

"This game brings emotions and you need to use them to your advantage.

"We've had a couple of games now that we went up and didn't play how we need to so I think that's a step forward.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Liverpool have been linked with a lot of players over the last few years.

Over £600 million has been spent on them and, more change is still needed.

Obviously, this isn't the outcome that the Anfield outfit will have wanted but, it's the hand that they've seemingly been dealt.

All of their rivals are constantly looking for ways to upgrade their team and, the more that they manage to do this, the better they become and the more difficult they are to beat.

Fans expected Liverpool to be competing for silverware this term but, now that feels like it all rests on their transfer plans with the club now being handed a green light to sign one of their targets.

Barcelona want to sign Ayden Heaven which could give Liverpool the green light to sign Ronald Araujo.

One of the main positions that Liverpool needed to upgrade in the 2026-27 transfer window was their defence.

Andy Robertson and Ibrahima Konate both exited Anfield for free and, the performances of Jeremie Frimpong and Conor Bradley were shoddy.

Throw in the fact that Bradley managed to suffer yet another long-term injury and, Liverpool were left with a bit-part defence.

That's why Jeremy Jacquet and Ronald Araujo were brought in.

Nobody knew how each defender would perform due to their lack of Premier League experience but, to the surprise of many, they've been two of the Reds' best players.

But, because Araujo is only on a season-long loan, his future is still undecided or, it was until this fresh patch from BBC Sport.

"Fulham and Barcelona are among the clubs to have expressed an interest in Heaven, with both having tried to sign him when he decided to leave Arsenal," they wrote.

"The England U20s defender's preference is believed to be a loan move, though he would also entertain permanent offers.

According to recent reports, "At United he has largely been used as a back-up option and, after enjoying a run in the team under former manager Ruben Amorim, he lost his place under Michael Carrick. He returned to the side only after an injury crisis hit the club last season.

"Heaven is also capable of playing at left-back and in midfield, but does not expect to be trusted as a regular starter amid the instability at Old Trafford, with the club 19th in the league.

"He is under contract until 2029 in a deal that includes an option for an extra year.".

Ayden Heaven joining Barcelona could force Barcelona to sell Ronald Araujo.

Araujo's versatility is one of the best things about him.

The defender can be comfortably used as a centre-back or a right-back with Iraola using him in both positions this term.

Indeed, the Uruguayan's injury history is a bit of a worry but, touch wood, he's managed to keep fit while playing for Liverpool so far.

As mentioned, Araujo's future isn't set in stone yet but, if Barca manage to sign Heaven from Manchester United, it feels like Araujo would fall further down Hansi Flick's plans.

This could mean that the La Liga giants are willing to negotiate a cheaper deal for the centre-back which, judging by the recent developments from Liverpool, is exactly what they want.

Here's hoping that a deal can be reached soon and that Barcelona find a successor for their captain soon.

By Carter White | 27 Nov 2026 14:53, Last updated: 27 Nov 2026 15:01.

Leeds United and Fulham have reportedly suffered a major blow to their respective pursuits of signing Racing de Santander striker Yassir Zabiri.

Daniel Farke's side have been in the business of getting their own house in order recently, announcing a contract extension for Japanese midfielder Ao Tanaka until the end of the 2028-29 campaign.

Leading Leeds' goalscoring ranks in the Premier League this term, Dominic Calvert-Lewin lead the way for the 28-year-old maestro, with the England international  also signing upcoming terms.

As for matters in West London, Alvaro Arbeloa's Fulham went down the La Liga route during the summer transfer window, looking to replace high-profile departures Raul Jimenez and Harry Wilson.

It was claimed earlier in the season that members of the Craven Cottage playing staff were unhappy with the situation at the club following the arrival of the former Real Madrid manager.

According to Spanish publication SER Cantabria via El Desmarque, Premier League clubs Leeds and Fulham have suffered a major blow in their potential pursuits of Zaibiri ahead of the January transfer window.

The 21-year-old is currently on loan at Racing Santander from French club Rennes, who supposedly have no option to recall the youngster from his spell in Spain until the end of the season.

The report states that Les Rennais would need to pay Racing Santander an 'extraordinary' amount of compensation to recall Zabiri during the January trading point - a move that would allow a permanent sale of the star.

Leeds, Fulham and Ipswich Town are the known Premier League suitors for the attacker, who recently made his Morocco senior debut during the November international break, scoring against Niger.

However, those English clubs could be blown out of the water by the other horses in this particular transfer race, with Spanish powerhouses Barcelona and Real Madrid noted to be interested in the talent.

Netting on 11 occasions across his opening 13 top-flight appearances of the season, Zabiri is only bested by Raphinha (15) and Kylian Mbappe (13) in La Liga's Golden Boot race after 13 games.

The 21-year-old burst onto the Racing Santander stage with a hat-trick against Elche in August before continuing his attacking antics into the autumn, recently bagging a brace in the victory over Real Sociedad.

The world-class form of Zabiri has caught the eye of some of Europe's biggest clubs, so it appears that the likes of Leeds and Fulham are set to be muscled out of a move for the Moroccan sensation.

Middle–Late Pleistocene Denisovans and unresolved Homo in southern China

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 54 min read (10722 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~54 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • The taxonomic classification of East Asian late Middle Pleistocene and early Late Pleistocene hominins has been a subject of intense debate.
  • However, morphological heterogeneity persists among these hominins, for instance, cranial capacities of approximately 1,700–1,800 ml and a Neanderthal-like temporal labyrinth configuration and/or the presence of a suprainiac fossa in Xuchang and Xujiayao, and a round orbit in Maba10,11,12.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Molecular and morphological evidence increasingly supports the view that most East Asian Middle to Late Pleistocene archaic Homo belong to Denisovans1, yet the presence of other contemporaneous lineages has remained unclear. Here we report a set of newly discovered hominin fossils (4 isolated teeth; more than 100.8 thousand years ago and 104.5–42.6 thousand years ago, respectively) from 2 cave sites (Chuanshandong and Longchuandong) in Guangxi, southern China. Integrated morphological and palaeoproteomic analyses reveal substantial phenotypic and molecular diversity consistent with at least two distinct lineages. One lineage (Longchuandong) is assigned to a Denisovan-affinity population, owing to its extreme similarity to Altai Denisovans with respect to dental morphology and single amino acid polymorphisms that match those of Denisovans from Harbin, Penghu, Bianfu Cave and Altai. The other lineage, represented by the Chuanshandong hominin, is an unresolved archaic Homo, as it carries an ancestral variant (AMELY 179M) shared with Homo antecessor and great apes and another variant (AMBN 253G) that is diagnostic of East Asian Middle Pleistocene Homo erectus but lacks the Denisovan-associated AMBN 273V variant (it being highly probable that this is inherited from H. erectus). Dental morphology in this lineage exhibits a mosaic of plesiomorphic and derived traits but no clear Denisovan affinity. These findings indicate that diverse hominin populations may have inhabited subtropical China during the Middle and Late Pleistocene, including a Denisovan-affinity population and another unresolved archaic Homo.

The taxonomic classification of East Asian late Middle Pleistocene and early Late Pleistocene hominins has been a subject of intense debate. These hominins are consistently characterized by plesiomorphic features, including a long and low neurocranium with a thick vault, a massive supraorbital torus, a sloping forehead and a robust mandible with a retreating symphysis, combined with derived traits such as an enlarged cranial capacity, a highly arched temporal squama, reduced prognathism and simplified dental morphology2,3,4,5. Phenotypic and molecular evidence has increasingly aligned these hominins with Denisovans2,6,7,8. For instance, the Harbin and Xujiayao crania, the Bianfu Cave radius, and the Xiahe and Penghu partial mandibles have been classified as Denisovan on the basis of palaeoproteomic and/or mitochondrial DNA analyses1,4,6,7,8,9. Phylogenetic studies based on trait matrices have linked Harbin Denisovans to Dali, Jinniushan, Hualongdong and Xiahe, suggesting a potentially broader distribution of Denisovans across mainland East Asia2.

However, morphological heterogeneity persists among these hominins, for instance, cranial capacities of approximately 1,700–1,800 ml and a Neanderthal-like temporal labyrinth configuration and/or the presence of a suprainiac fossa in Xuchang and Xujiayao, and a round orbit in Maba10,11,12. Such variations have led to the proposal of distinct species, that is, pre-modern Homo sapiens, Homo juluensis and a Neanderthal-related lineage13,14,15,16,17. Moreover, most specimens attributed to the Denisovan assemblage have originated from northern and central China, with few contemporaneous hominin fossils reported from southern China, particularly subtropical regions. Thus, it remains unclear whether the East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo represent only Denisovans or multiple lineages adapted to diverse environments across a vast territory.

According to recent reports, resolution of this question requires the discovery of more hominin fossils dating to the Denisovan period, especially from regions where such remains have not yet been reported. A comprehensive comparative study centred on such fossils should be conducted, incorporating a wide range of Eurasian Homo samples to establish a robust evolutionary framework for taxonomic identification. In addition to morphological comparisons, molecular analyses are essential for accurate taxonomic assignment. However, ancient DNA preservation is poor in the warm, humid conditions of southern China, particularly for late Middle Pleistocene specimens4,18,19. In such cases, palaeoproteomic analysis offers a vital complementary approach. This technology has been successfully applied to the identification of Denisovan specimens from diverse environments (including the Xiahe partial mandible4 and rib20 from the high-altitude Tibetan Plateau; the Penghu partial mandible6 from the Taiwan strait; the Bianfu Cave partial parietal bones, radius and teeth9 from southwest China; the Xujiayao cranium and mandible1 from north China; and the Harbin cranium7 from the plain of northeast China) and the phylogenetic placement of Homo antecessor (approximately 949–772 thousand years ago (ka)) and East Asian Middle Pleistocene Homo erectus21,22.

A group of hominin fossils has been recovered from two sites in Nanning (Chuanshandong in Long’an County) and Liuzhou (Longchuandong in Luzhai County) within the karst terrain of Guangxi, a region renowned for its rich Pleistocene mammalian fossils, during surveys of late Middle Pleistocene cave deposits by our interdisciplinary team since 2016 (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1). These investigations spanned an area extending more than 500 km from Chongzuo City in the southwest to Guilin City in the northeast. The discovery of these new hominin remains in this area will be critical for clarification of the geographical distribution of Denisovans and assessment of whether multiple archaic Homo lineages existed in mainland East Asia during the Middle and Late Pleistocene.

a, Geographical locations. b,c, Blueprint views of Chuanshandong in Long’an (b) and Longchuandong in Luzhai (c). d,e, Photograph (d) and schematic (e) showing stratigraphic deposition at Chuanshandong. Red stars in a indicate the locations of two cave sites in this study, while red stars in b, c and e indicate the locations where hominin teeth were recovered. Base map data in a from Natural Earth (https://www.naturalearthdata.com). Scale bars, 5 m (b), 10 m (c).

According to recent reports, here we present direct U-series dating results for hominin teeth from Chuanshandong and Longchuandong (more than 100.8 ka and 104.5–42.6 ka, respectively), the optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) ages of the hominin fossil-bearing layer (between 49.5 ± 2.6 ka and 34.2 ± 4.1 ka) and a biostratigraphic chronology based on the faunal assemblage (late Middle to early Late Pleistocene age, younger than 300 ka). To determine the taxonomic affinity of the hominins, we performed detailed morphological descriptions and comprehensive metric and non-metric comparisons with a broader range of Eurasian Homo specimens. In addition, we conducted palaeoproteomic analyses of hominin teeth and compared the results with published data from H. erectus, H. antecessor, Denisovans, Neanderthals and H. sapiens to further clarify the taxonomic affinity of these new hominins. The integration of these approaches will enhance our knowledge of the diversity of the East Asian late Middle Pleistocene hominins.

Chuanshandong lies in the karst terrain of Long’an County, Guangxi (Fig. 1). Two hominin teeth and associated abundant mammalian teeth were recovered from layer 3 of an approximately 1.2-m-thick consolidated deposit adhering to the cave walls of the western chamber entrance, the bottom deposit of which was eroded (Fig. 1, Supplementary Text 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1). The sedimentary sequence consisted of the following six layers, from top to bottom: yellowish-brown sand (layer 1), consolidated brown calcareous-cemented sand (layer 2), greyish-brown sandy silt (layer 3), yellowish-brown brecciated sand (layer 4), brown gravel-bearing clayey silt (level 5) and yellowish-brown gravel-bearing silt (level 6). The two hominin teeth were separated from each other by approximately 5 cm vertically and 20 cm horizontally within layer 3. The deposit in layer 3 consisted of homogeneous, fine-grained particles without lamination, with grain-size and size distributions similar to those of modern soil near the cave entrance. They were all polymodal, mostly dominated by the clay fraction with very low proportions of particles larger than 63 μm (less than 8.4%) and relatively low percentages of coarse fraction (Supplementary Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 1). This suggested that the deposit of layer 3 was derived from the modern soil outside and transported by low-energy, intermittent and short-term water activity. The hominin and mammal fossils from layer 3 were dominated by isolated teeth and may have been transported gradually into the inner cave by slope gravitation resulting from a depth gradient of approximately 5 m between the cave entrance and the burial location of the teeth. Therefore, the burial age of the fossils may substantially lag behind their true age.

Longchuandong is situated in the karst landscape of Luzhai County, Guangxi (Fig. 1). Two isolated hominin teeth and numerous faunal remains were discovered in the brownish-yellow clay (Fig. 1, Supplementary Text 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1). Given that most fossils from Longchuandong are isolated teeth, the fossils were highly likely to have been sorted and transported into the deep cave by water. No stone artefacts or other cultural relics were associated with hominin fossils at these two sites.

Industry observers note that to estimate the ages of these hominin teeth, we applied both laser-ablation-based and classic isotope-dilution-based U-series dating analyses to the hominin and associated mammalian teeth (Supplementary Text 2, Supplementary Figs. 3–5 and Supplementary Tables 2 and 3). The lower right third premolar (P3) from Chuanshandong yielded laser ablation U-series ages ranging from 72.2 ± 1.4 ka to 63.8 ± 1.3 ka and an isotope-dilution-based age of 62.1 ± 0.3 ka. The left P3 yielded laser ablation U-series ages ranging from 109.2 ± 2.7 ka to 97.7 ± 4.6 ka and an isotope-dilution-based U-series age of 100.8 ± 0.2 ka. These two P3s could have originated from one individual, considering their similar morphology and degree of occlusal wear (minimum number of individuals = 1). The isotope-dilution-based U-series age of 100.8 ka thus provides a minimum age for the Chuanshandong. This age was also included in the range of the laser-ablation-based U-series ages of the associated mammal teeth (211.1–37.8 ka) (Supplementary Figs. 6–8 and Supplementary Table 4). However, the OSL ages of the hominin fossil-bearing layer in Chuanshandong ranged from 49.5 ± 2.6 ka to 34.2 ± 4.1 ka; that is, they were significantly younger than the U-series ages of the hominin teeth and most mammalian fossils, suggesting slow transportation or delayed burial of these materials (Supplementary Text 3, Supplementary Fig. 9 and Supplementary Table 5).

The upper right second molar from Longchuandong (M2) yielded laser-ablation-based U-series ages of 46.9 ± 2.2 ka to 37.7 ± 2.0 ka and an isotope-dilution-based age of 42.6 ± 0.4 ka, whereas the lower right fourth premolar (P4) from the same layer returned laser ablation ages of 111.0 ± 3.6 ka to 96.7 ± 3.5 ka and an isotope-dilution-based age of 104.5 ± 0.4 ka. These ages fell within the range of the laser-ablation-based U-series ages of the associated mammal teeth (160.4–30.1 ka) (Supplementary Figs. 10 and 11 and Supplementary Table 6). Associated faunal remains from both sites represented a typical Ailuropoda-Stegodon fauna (Supplementary Figs. 12 and 13). The presence of Elephas maximus and Tapirus indicus, together with the relatively small tooth size of Ailuropoda in Chuanshandong and T. indicus in Longchuandong, all indicate a late Middle to Late Pleistocene age (younger than 300 ka). Despite the limitations of each dating method, the integration of U-series, OSL and biostratigraphic context supports a Middle and Late Pleistocene age for the Chuanshandong and Longchuandong hominins.

Sources indicate that we described the dental morphology of a pair of P3s from Chuanshandong and one P4 and one M2 from Longchuandong and compared them with a broad range of Homo specimens (including H. erectus, East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo, Denisovans, Neanderthals and H. sapiens) to determine their taxonomy (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Tables 7–11). These materials occupied an intermediate morphological position between H. erectus and H. sapiens, characterized by a mosaic of dental traits and the absence of autapomorphic Neanderthal features. Nevertheless, the two assemblages exhibited distinct phenotypic profiles.

a,b, Longchuandong M2 (a) and Longchuandong P4 (b) from Luzhai. c,d, Chuanshandong left (c) and right (d) P3s from Long’an. The fossils and virtual reconstructions of the EDJ (shown in cyan) are displayed in the following order: occlusal, mesial and lingual views. B, buccal; M, mesial; D, distal. Scale bar, 5 mm.

Sources indicate that the first phenotypic pattern was represented by the P4 and M2 of Longchuandong hominins. These individuals resembled the East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo with respect to both M2 and P4 morphology and exhibited notable affinity to Denisova 4 from Denisova Cave (Altai) in terms of M2 characteristics (Figs. 2 and 3, Supplementary Text 4 and Supplementary Figs. 14–17). Their P4s shared an approximately symmetrical buccal and lingual contour (unlike the mesiobuccal protruding contour typical of H. erectus and distolingual protruding contour typical of Neanderthals) and non-tapering roots (distinct from the tapering roots of H. sapiens)3,23,24 (Supplementary Fig. 17). Their M2s had comparable hypocone size, similar enamel–dentine junction (EDJ) shape and a non-dendritic EDJ surface, distinct from the tall crown topography and the absence of a hypocone or only ridge-like hypocone of H. sapiens, and from the symmetrically trapezoidal EDJ viewed occlusally and dendritic EDJ surface of H. erectus23,25,26,27,28,29,30,31 (Fig. 3, Supplementary Fig. 15 and Supplementary Table 12). The Longchuandong M2 did not exhibit clear variation compared with Neanderthals, especially in diffeomorphic surface matching analyses of EDJ shape (the typicality probabilities of being classified as Neanderthals were 42.13% and 39.11% in the between-group principal component analysis and canonical variate analysis, respectively), although Neanderthals tend to be characterized by a more skewed M2 crown viewed occlusally and a higher occurrence of transverse crest (23.5% in early and late Neanderthals)28,32 (Fig. 3 and Supplementary Table 12). In particular, the Longchuandong M2 most closely resembled Denisova 4 from Denisova Cave (Altai) when all dental features analysed were considered, including the two-dimensional crown outline shape and three-dimensional EDJ shape, in addition to the crown size, relative hypocone size and degree of elevation of the crista obliqua, which overlap among different taxonomic groups to varying degrees33,34,35 (Supplementary Figs. 15, 18 and 19).

The magnitude of displacement between the global mean shape and each extreme conformation is shown as a colour map from dark blue (contracted) to red (bulged).

It has been revealed that the second phenotype was represented by the paired P3s of the Chuanshandong hominin and did not align well with any established East Asian Homo member. These samples retained an erectus-like short EDJ that could be clearly distinguished from that of Neanderthals and H. sapiens and a complex root system with approximately constant root breadth from cervix to apex, which is normally found in H. erectus (for instance, the single Tomes’s root with bifurcated apex in Zhoukoudian and two-rooted pattern in Sangiran) but rarely occurs in Neanderthals or H. sapiens28,36,37,38,39 (Figs. 2 and 3, Supplementary Text 4, Supplementary Figs. 20–22 and Supplementary Table 13). However, the Chuanshandong P3s exhibited derived traits that were shared with other later Homo and distinct from those of H. erectus: reduced crown asymmetry, less pronounced distolingual protrusion, a lingually displaced polygon area, absent metaconid apex (probably sharper protoconid dentine horn) and a less crenulated mesial vertical groove on the buccal surface40,41. They were distinguishable from the East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo from Panxian Dadong, which falls within the H. sapiens range, with a slightly asymmetrical crown and tall EDJ topography, despite a non-tapering root42 (Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. 22).

It has been revealed that to provide molecular evidence for taxonomy and sex attribution, we conducted ancient protein extraction on three of the hominin samples: Longchuandong M2, Longchuandong P4 and Chuanshandong right P3. After searching against the Hominidae enamel database, we removed peptides that were detected in the extraction blank or attributed to contaminant proteins to control contamination from the experiment; this resulted in 2,894, 2,038 and 2,099 identified peptides for the three samples, respectively. The endogeneity of the proteome was supported by high deamidation rates of asparagine and glutamine, as well as relatively short peptide length caused by degradation (Fig. 4). We evaluated the replicate consistency by calculating the shared and specific peptide counts between two runs of liquid chromatography coupled with tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) for each fraction from these teeth, as well as two fractions from Longchuandong P4 (Supplementary Table 14). Although more than 50% of total peptides were shared, indicating some replicate consistency, specific peptides from each run or fraction accounted for 40% or more in total; this demonstrated the necessity of conducting multiple runs or collecting multiple fractions to improve the coverage of recovered proteome. To avoid misassignment, we removed peptides matching multiple genes, and a typical enamel-specific proteome was retrieved from the three hominin samples (Supplementary Table 15). Abundant amelogenin, Y isoform (AMELY)-specific peptides indicated that all were from male individuals. We further inspected the phylogenetically informative single amino acid polymorphisms (SAPs) to determine their population assignments by validation with BLASTp, assessment of peptide depth across three software tools, evaluation of spectral quality and quantification of deamidation rates (Methods, Table 1, Supplementary Text 5, Supplementary Table 16, Supplementary Data 1 and 2 and Supplementary Figs. 23–28).

The data analysis process for published archaic individuals was the same as that used for the Chuanshandong and Longchuandong samples, except that for Laos TNH2-1, H. antecessor (Atapuerca) and H. erectus (Dmanisi), we used an expanded database with the main dentine collagens (COL1A1, COL1A2 and COL2A1). Recent findings suggest that both the Longchuandong M2 and P4 exhibited ameloblastin (AMBN) 273V (55 and 59 supporting peptides; Table 1), which is shared with East Asian Middle Pleistocene H. erectus, Harbin, Penghu, Bianfu Cave, Denisova 25 and Denisova 3, and with some H. sapiens from Southeast Asia and Oceania with high levels of Denisovan introgression6,9,22,43,44,45. In phylogenetic analysis, the two Longchuandong samples were grouped with Denisova 3 with 100% support (Supplementary Text 6 and Supplementary Fig. 29). Given the age of the samples and the morphological similarity between the Longchuandong M2 and Denisova 4 from Altai Denisova Cave, the Longchuandong samples are likely to represent a Denisovan-affinity lineage in south China.

According to recent reports, unlike the two Longchuandong samples, Chuanshandong carried a SAP, AMBN 253G, supported by nine peptides (Table 1), among which seven peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) had a complete series of y- and b-ions surrounding the SAP. This SAP has been reported in three groups of late H. erectus from Zhoukoudian, Hexian and Sunjiadong22, but all other comparative specimens in Hominidae present AMBN 253A, including H. antecessor from Atapuerca21, H. erectus from Dmanisi21, Harbin7, Penghu6, Bianfu Cave9, TNH2-1 from Laos46, Denisova 3 (ref. 43), Denisova 25 (ref. 45), 9 Neanderthals47,48,49,50,51,52, Ust’-Ishim53, H. sapiens and non-human great apes. In addition, AMELY 179M, an ancestral variant that is shared with H. antecessor21 and non-human great apes but not with H. sapiens, Neanderthals or the Denisovan clade, was also identified in Chuanshandong with seven supporting peptides (Table 1); among these, two PSMs had two b-ions bracketing the SAP, and eight PSMs had one b-ion when the SAP was located at the amino terminus. Phylogenetic analysis indicated that Chuanshandong formed a sister group to the common ancestors of Neanderthals, Denisovans and H. sapiens (posterior probability: 100%; Supplementary Fig. 29). The integrated evidence indicates that Chuanshandong may belong to a lineage distinct from the Denisovan in mainland southern China.

The scarcity of hominin fossils from subtropical southern China during the Middle to Late Pleistocene transition has hampered our understanding of the geographical distribution of Denisovans and the potential existence of other Homo lineages in mainland East Asia. Here we report 4 isolated hominin teeth from Guangxi (Chuanshandong and Longchuandong), dated to at least 100.8 ka and 104.5–42.6 ka, respectively. These ages establish the specimens as contemporaries of northern Denisovans (approximately 300–45 ka)4,7,8,20,54,55 that provide important fossil evidence of non-sapiens Homo in subtropical regions adjacent to southeast Asia during this interval. Although both the Chuanshandong and Longchuandong hominins exhibited a mosaic of plesiomorphic and derived traits, palaeoproteomic analysis revealed variations in AMBN 253 and 273, as well in as AMELY 179, which allowed phylogenetic placement of these samples. The results indicate that at least two non-sapiens Homo populations may have existed in southern China’s subtropics during the Middle and Late Pleistocene.

Among these diverse populations, the Longchuandong materials provide compelling evidence for the presence of a Denisovan-affinity population in subtropical southern China. Compared with H. erectus and H. sapiens, the Longchuandong more closely resembled other East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo, Altai Denisova 4 and Neanderthals with respect to M2 morphology but could be differentiated from Neanderthals by its P4 features. These two specimens carried the AMBN 273V variant found in Harbin, Penghu, Bianfu Cave and Altai Denisovans, whereas Neanderthals and most H. sapiens carry the AMBN 273M variant6,7,9,43,44,47,48,49,53. These integrated morphological and molecular data together support the identification of Denisovan-affinity populations in subtropical southern China. In previous enamel proteomic studies, AMBN 273 was found to be polymorphic in Denisovans, with the M variant in Laos TNH2-1, M/V in Denisova 25 and Harbin, and V in Longchuandong, Penghu, Bianfu Cave and Denisova 3 (refs. 6,9,22,43,45,46), indicating regional variation of molecular characteristics within this lineage. Taking the Longchuandong finding into account, there is evidence that Denisovans were distributed in Siberia, northern China, the Tibetan Plateau, the Taiwan Strait, subtropical southern China and tropical Laos, suggesting their possible adaptability to diverse environments, from cold and arid high-altitude plateaus to hot and humid low-altitude regions4,6,7,8,9,20,46,56,57. Neanderthals have not been discovered in regions with confirmed Denisovan distribution other than Siberia. Given their widely separated geographical regions, the morphological similarity between Longchuandong Denisovans and Neanderthals (for instance, with respect to M2) does not necessarily indicate hybridization. Instead, it may simply reflect the limited diagnostic value of certain anatomical features in distinguishing these two taxa. Unlike the similarity in M2 morphology, Denisovans and Neanderthals can be effectively differentiated by other dental traits, such as the crown shape of P4 and M1, the labial convexity and tuberculum dentale of I1, and other cranial and mandibular traits1.

Sources indicate that in contrast to Longchuandong, the remains from Chuanshandong were marked by an ancestral variant (AMELY 179M) shared with H. antecessor and great apes and another variant (AMBN 253G) shared with East Asian Middle Pleistocene H. erectus but absent from contemporaneous Denisovans, Neanderthals and H. sapiens. In addition, Chuanshandong retained a plesiomorphic short crown and complex roots, differing notably from Neanderthals, H. sapiens and the Panxian Dadong (which is considered to be potentially Denisovan on the basis of broader dental comparisons with other East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo)42. Although Chuanshandong differed from East Asian H. erectus in having more progressive dental features and in the presence of AMBN 273M, the fact that they shared AMBN 253G implies that they may be related. The presence of an ancestral variant (AMELY 179M) and an erectus-like variant (AMBN 253G) suggests that the Chuanshandong hominin belongs to a primitive Homo lineage that may have survived into the Late Pleistocene in a geographical refugium. Admixture among existing archaic Homo in southern China or gene flow from H. erectus are plausible explanations for the unique molecular and morphological attributes of Chuanshandong hominin.

The findings of this study show that the subtropical area in southern China may have hosted multiple populations of archaic Homo during the Middle and Late Pleistocene. In addition to the previously suggested Neanderthal-related hominin at Maba in the adjacent Guangdong Province16,17,58, we have now identified both a Denisovan-affinity hominin and another unresolved non-sapiens archaic Homo in this region. However, such phylogenetic inference based on the limited proteomic data is preliminary. More molecular data accumulated in the future, spanning broad geographical regions and time periods, and including ancient DNA from these archaic hominins, will provide us with a better understanding of the taxonomic value of specific proteomic mutations or variants and their variability between archaic and modern populations. Moreover, key diagnostic characteristics, especially trait combinations that significantly vary among different taxa, should be systematically screened from the relatively rich morphological dataset to define a lineage. Finally, it will be crucial to propose possible interpretations that can account for both morphological diversity and molecular variability, to further illustrate the framework of human evolution in East Asia.

Recent findings suggest that A sliding calliper was used to measure the mesiodistal and buccolingual dimensions of the hominin teeth, with recordings taken to the nearest 0.1 mm. We applied the terminology and grading criteria of the Arizona State University Dental Anthropology System59, as well as the standards of Martinón-Torres et al.28, to describe and score crown characteristics, including the hypocone size, the crista obliqua, the transverse crest of the upper molar and the transverse crest of the lower premolar. Root structures of lower premolars were scored using Wood’s system60. The Chuanshandong and Longchuandong hominins were compared mainly with East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo or Denisovans, East Asian/Southeast Asian H. erectus, Homo heidelbergensis, early and late Neanderthals and H. sapiens.

To quantify the crown contour shape, cusp and fovea arrangement, and main occlusal groove orientation of the M2 and P3, we conducted two-dimensional geometric morphometric analyses on the basis of occlusal photographs of the teeth oriented in anatomical position following the procedure introduced in refs. 32,40. All specimens were digitally mirrored to the same antimeres as the Chuanshandong and Longchuandong specimens in Adobe Photoshop 12.0 when they were from the opposite side. Before semilandmark placement, the interproximal wear facet was digitally restored to its original state according to the extent of wear and the profile of the neighbouring contour.

For the P3 analysis, four landmarks were placed at the anterior fovea, posterior fovea, protoconid apex and metaconid apex. Forty equidistant semilandmarks were defined along the crown contour. For the M2, three landmarks were placed at the intersections of the buccal and central grooves with each other and with the crown contour. These landmarks delineated four distinct curves along the crown contour and in the occlusal grooves. Each of them was divided into different and equidistant segments, and the dividing points were designated as semilandmarks. In total, 3 landmarks and 36 semilandmarks were defined on the occlusal surface of M2.

Recent findings suggest that landmark and semilandmark coordinates were digitized using TpsDig2 v.2.12 (https://www.sbmorphometrics.org/soft-dataacq.html)61. Procrustes superimposition (minimizing Procrustes distances) was performed on the raw coordinates using the geomorph package (v.3.5)62. Principal component analysis was then conducted on the resulting shape variables. The ggplot package (v.4.0.3)63 was used to produce a scatter plot of principal component 1 against principal component 2 for visualization of morphological variation among different taxonomic groups.

Recent findings suggest that the teeth from Chuanshandong and Longchuandong were scanned using the Phoenix V|tome|x M microfocus CT cabinet system at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, Chinese Academy of Sciences. The scanning parameters were as follows: 160 kV, 120 μA, isotropic voxel size of 34.20 µm, 0.2-mm-thick copper filter. Microcomputed tomography data of Neanderthals from Krapina were downloaded from the NESPOS database64. Tomographic slices in TIFF format were imported into Mimics v.17.0 (Materialise, https://www.materialise.com) for segmentation of enamel and dentine and virtual reconstruction of the pulp cavity. The resulting EDJ was exported in STL format for subsequent shape analysis. The worn dentine horn apices of Longchuandong M2 and Chuanshandong P3s were restored by two observers independently following a geometric method validated in previous studies in Avizo v.9.2 (https://www.thermofisher.com/amira-avizo)65 (Supplementary Fig. 30).

In a recent development, the three-dimensional EDJ models were imported into Avizo 9.2, and all specimens were superimposed using the ‘Align Surface’ function. Following superimposition, the STL files were saved and converted into VTK format using ParaView v.5.6.0 (https://www.paraview.org/). The VTK files were then read into Deformetrica v.4.3 (https://gitlab.com/icm-institute/aramislab/deformetrica) for quantification of deformations among the EDJ surfaces, modelled as diffeomorphisms66. Control points and momenta encoding the deformation parameters were generated and imported into R v.4.1.0 (https://www.r-project.org/)67. Principal component analysis, between-group principal component analysis and canonical variate analysis were performed using the following packages: RToolsForDeformetrica v.0.1 (ref. 68), ade4 v.1.7-17 (ref. 69), Morpho v.2.8 (ref. 70), gtools v.3.9.5 (ref. 71) and freesurferformats v.0.1.15 (ref. 72). Two sets of EDJ, independently reconstructed by two authors, were also analysed, and the results were compared to provide an indication of the reliability of the virtual reconstructions of the worn dentine horns (Supplementary Fig. 31).

Six samples were collected from the fossil-bearing layer of the Chuanshandong section, as well as two samples from the modern soil near the cave entrance, for grain-size analysis. Bulk samples were first treated with 30% hydrogen peroxide to remove organic matter, followed by 10% hydrochloric acid to remove carbonates. Subsequently, the samples were dispersed with 0.5 N sodium hexametaphosphate. Grain-size was measured using a Malvern Mastersizer 3000 particle analyser with an analytical precision of less than 1%.

High-resolution U-series in situ analysis using laser ablation system coupled with multi-collector inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA–MC-ICP-MS) was conducted to directly date the Chuanshandong and Longchuandong hominin teeth. Laser ablation was performed using an NWRimageGEO high-energy laser ablation system (Elemental Scientific Lasers), and mass spectrometry was performed with a Neoma MC-ICP-MS system (Thermo Scientific). A high-precision MC-ICP-MS U-series dating method using solution nebulization after chromatographic separation was also applied to hominin teeth as an accuracy test. Integration of both procedures provided a minimum age for the hominins at Chuanshandong and Longchuandong. Laser-ablation-based U-series analyses were also conducted on freshly cut cross-sections of associated mammalian teeth recovered from the same stratigraphic layer within a 1-m radius of the hominin teeth (Chuanshandong). These analyses were carried out at Nanjing Normal University and the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, using the LA–MC-ICP-MS methods described in ref. 73 and the solution method described in ref. 74.

Industry observers note that the age of the hominin teeth from Chuanshandong was constrained by optical dating of the hominin fossil-bearing sediments. Three sediment samples were collected using stainless steel tubes (20 cm long, with a diameter of 5 cm) hammered horizontally into a freshly dug vertical stratigraphic section. The tubes were immediately sealed with aluminium foil, wrapped with black plastic bags and taped to prevent light exposure and moisture loss. Sediment from the light-exposed end of each tube was separated and used for dose rate measurements, and material from the middle was used for equivalent dose (De) measurements. Sample preparation followed standard procedures described previously75. Coarse-grained quartz (90 μm to 150 μm) was extracted for De measurements.

Sources indicate that luminescence measurements were performed on a Risø Model DA-20 TL/OSL reader equipped with a 90Sr/90Y beta source for irradiation76 and an EMI 9235QA photomultiplier tube. Blue light-emitting diode stimulation (470 ± 30 nm) was used at 90% of 50 mW cm−2 full power, and 7.5 mm Hoya U-340 filters (transmission between 290 nm and 370 nm) were used for the quartz OSL measurements. The single-aliquot regenerative-dose protocol was used to determine the De (refs. 77,78) (Supplementary Table 17).

Sources indicate that the uranium, thorium and potassium concentrations of the three samples were measured by inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry and used to calculate the environmental dose rate. In situ water content (moist mass/dry mass) was determined by weighing samples before and after drying and assigned an absolute uncertainty of ±5%. Elemental concentrations were converted into an effective dose rate using the revised dose rate conversion factors79 and water content attenuation factors80. The cosmic dose contribution was estimated on the basis of the burial depth of the sample, the thickness of the overlying cave roof (approximately 30 m), the zenith-angle dependence of cosmic rays, and the latitude, longitude and altitude of the site81. Final dose rates and deposition ages were calculated using DRAC82. Details of sample preparation, measurement and data analysis are provided in Supplementary Text 3.

According to recent reports, microinvasive acid etching was conducted on the tooth enamel for protein extraction, using an approach modified from a published protocol83. After cleaning with a disposable toothbrush, the tooth was wrapped with parafilm with the small etching region exposed. Then, the etching region was washed with 3% hydrogen peroxide for 30 s and rinsed with ultrapure water. We conducted an initial etch of 2 min by placing the etching region on to the 5% (v/v) hydrochloric acid solution in the cap of a 1.5-ml microcentrifuge tube. This etch solution was discarded. Then, a second etch of 15 min was performed twice in the cap of another microcentrifuge tube, and the etch solutions were combined. After desalting with C18 ZipTips (Thermo Fisher Scientific), the peptides were eluted into 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid in 80% acetonitrile. The eluted solution was further vacuum-evaporated before being subjected to LC–MS/MS analysis.

In a recent development, A Neolithic human tooth from the Xiawanggang Site (approximately 5 ka) in Henan Province, China, was chosen as a positive control sample (referred to as ‘Xiawanggang’). The positive control sample and a blank extraction (negative control sample) were processed in the same batch as the hominin samples with the same protocol. All sample treatments were performed in the dedicated clean room for ancient protein analysis in the Molecular Paleontology Laboratory at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, Chinese Academy of Sciences. To evaluate the replicate consistency and improve the coverage of recovered proteome, we etched two spots on Longchuandong P4 and obtained two fractions. Two LC–MS/MS runs were conducted for each fraction from these teeth.

The eluted peptides were analysed in data-dependent acquisition mode on an Orbitrap Exploris 480 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) interfaced with an Easy n-LC 1200 HPLC system (Thermo Scientific) at the Central Laboratory, Capital Medical University, Beijing, China. A trap column (100 μm i.d. × 2 cm, C18) and analytical column (150 μm i.d. × 15 cm, C18) were used, both packed in-house with 3 μm reversed-phase silica (Reprosil-Pur C18 AQ, Dr. Maisch GmbH). Mobile phase A was 0.1% formic acid in water, and mobile phase B was 0.1% formic acid in 80% acetonitrile. The peptides were separated using a 125-min linear gradient program (0–1 min, 1–9% B; 1–101 min, 9–28% B; 101–113 min, 28–42% B; 113–117 min, 42–99% B; 117–125 min, 99% B) at a flow rate of 350 nl min−1. For the mass spectrometry, full scans were measured with a m/z range from 350 to 1,500, a resolution of 60,000, an AGC target of 300% and a maximum injection time of 50 ms. The precursors were selected for higher-energy collisional dissociation fragmentation with an isolation window of 1.6 m/z and a dynamic exclusion of 60 s. MS2 scans were obtained with a resolution of 15,000, a normalized collision energy of 30%, an AGC target of 75% and a maximum injection time of 22 ms.

All the raw data files from the hominin samples, as well as those from the positive and negative control samples, were searched using PEAKS Online (v.11.5)84, MaxQuant (v.2.6.0.0)85 and pFind (v.3.2.2)86. Multiple rounds of target database searching were supplemented with searching of a contaminant database used in a previous publication7.

First, the data were searched against the entire human reference proteome downloaded from UniProt (proteome ID UP000005640, accessed on 20 May 2022) using PEAKS Online, including peptide de novo, PEAKS DB, PTM and SPIDER. The precursor ion mass tolerance and fragment ion mass tolerance were set to 10 ppm and 0.02 Da, respectively. Unspecific digestion was chosen. Deamidation (NQ), oxidation (M), hydroxylation (P), phosphorylation (STY), pyro-Glu from E and pyro-Glu from Q were set as variable modifications, and a maximum of three modifications were allowed for each peptide. The peptide length was set from 6 to 45. A false discovery rate of 1% at the spectral level was used to filter the results. Proteins were accepted if at least two peptides were present. Main enamel proteins were identified in the hominin samples, whereas no dentine-related collagens were detected. This was not unexpected, because the acid etch approach can only extract proteins from the superficial enamel and cannot access deeper layers such as dentine. Thus, dentine collagens were excluded from further analysis.

According to recent reports, A second round of database searching was conducted using three software tools against a custom-built database, referred to as the ‘Hominidae enamel database’ in this study. This database was composed of sequences for 12 main enamel proteins: amelogenin, X isoform (AMELX), AMELY, AMBN, enamelin (ENAM), amelotin (AMTN), odontogenic ameloblast-associated protein (ODAM), matrix metalloproteinase 20 (MMP20), kallikrein 4 (KLK4), tuftelin (TUFT1), collagen α1(XVII) chain (COL17A1), albumin (ALB) and α2-HS-glycoprotein (AHSG). Species were restricted to Hominidae, including archaic hominins such as Denisovans and Neanderthals. Protein sequences, including canonical and isoform sequences, were downloaded from UniProt and obtained from the translated Hominid Palaeoproteomic Reference Dataset available at Zenodo87. Previously published protein sequences from extinct archaic hominins (H. antecessor, H. erectus, Penghu)6,21,22, Paranthropus88 and Gigantopithecus89 were also incorporated. The parameters for data searching on PEAKS Online were the same as those used in the initial search against the entire human reference proteome. The parameters for MaxQuant and pFind were similar, with a few adjustments: for MaxQuant, phosphorylation (STY) was excluded from the variable modifications, the PSM and protein false discovery rates were set to 1% and 10%, respectively, and the ion tolerance and maximum number of modifications for each peptide were set to default values; and for pFind, hydroxylation (K) was also set as a variable modification, and open search was enabled. The possible mutations identified by PEAKS SPIDER and pFind open search were added to the original database for iterative data search and validation.

After removal of peptides detected in the negative control sample or assigned to contaminant proteins, we used the remaining peptides from each hominin and positive control sample to calculate deamidation profiles to support their endogeneity90.

After excluding SAPs that were supported by a single peptide or indistinguishable owing to post-translational modifications7, we manually checked the variants within the Homo genus that met initial thresholds (PSM count ≥ 2, PSM ratio ≥ 10% and intensity ratio ≥ 10%) to confirm their reliability6,7,88. The criteria were as follows.

BLASTp: first, all the supporting peptides were submitted to BLASTp search against the NCBInr database. Peptides that also matched proteins from other genes or from some archaeal, bacterial or fungal species were removed from further evaluation and calculation.

Depth across different software: after BLAST filtration, variants were retained for further consideration only if each software tool retained at least two peptides.

According to recent reports, MS2 support: we manually inspected the MS2 spectra of all supporting PSMs to confirm the presence of y- and b-ions around the SAP. Two levels of criteria were applied: ‘MS2 support’ required at least one y- or b-ion linked to the SAP, whereas ‘strict MS2 support’ required at least two y-ions or two b-ions bracketing the SAP. An exception was made for terminal SAPs, for which a single associated ion was accepted for the strict classification. The number of peptides meeting each criterion was then calculated.

Deamidation rate: using peptides containing asparagine or glutamine residues, we calculated deamidation levels on the basis of spectral count and ion intensity. The number of PSMs and total count of covered N and Q sites were also recorded. An elevated deamidation rate in these peptides suggested an endogenous origin, which reinforced the reliability of the SAP identification.

Using these criteria, we evaluated eight positions across the three hominin samples (Supplementary Data 2) and confidently identified four of them. One of these was AMELY 59M, a male-specific SAP commonly used for sex identification83; details of the other three reliable SAPs are shown in Table 1.

We combined the overlapping results from the three software tools and used them to generate consensus sequences for each protein from the three hominin samples with Biopython (v.1.83)91. For sites with more than two amino acid variants, we calculated the number of PSMs, the PSM ratio and the intensity ratio for each variant. In PEAKS Online and MaxQuant, a variant was considered to be reliable if it met all of the following thresholds: PSM count ≥ 2, PSM ratio ≥ 10% and intensity ratio ≥ 10% (ref. 7). In pFind, the intensity ratio was discarded. Confident heterozygous positions were identified as those for which multiple amino acid variants passed these filters. On the basis of the overlapping results from the three tools, no heterozygous positions were retained in the three hominin samples. Amino acid variants supported by a single peptide were excluded. The unreliable phylogenetically informative SAPs inspected above were also marked as ‘X’ in the consensus sequences. Finally, the consensus sequences of six proteins, AMELX, AMELY, AMBN, ENAM, COL17A1 and ALB, were reconstructed.

The comparative dataset contained four archaic individuals, five extant great ape species, a gibbon (Nomascus leucogenys) and a macaque (Macaca mulatta). The protein sequences of four archaic individuals were obtained from the Hominid Palaeoproteomic Reference Dataset87; these individuals comprised Denisova 3, Altai Neanderthal, Chagyrskaya 8 and Vindija33.19. Protein sequences for extant great apes and other primates were retrieved from UniProt and NCBI (Supplementary Table 18). The six proteins were aligned using MAFFT (v.7.490)92 and concatenated with R package phylotools (v.0.2.2; https://github.com/helixcn/phylotools), resulting in a dataset with a total length of 4,108 amino acid positions. We also detected 16.67%, 14.51% and 14.68% non-missing sites in Longchuandong M2, Longchuandong P4 and Chuanshandong P3, respectively. Leucines were converted into isoleucines, as these two amino acids are isobaric and were indistinguishable in the tandem mass spectrometry used in this study.

Industry observers note that we performed phylogenetic analysis on the aligned dataset using MrBayes (v.3.2.6)93. The best partitioning schemes and substitution models were chosen using PartitionFinder (v.2.1.1)94. Two Markov chain Monte Carlo runs were performed for 10,000,000 generations, with sampling every 5,000 generations. Convergence was evaluated using the average standard deviation of split frequencies and log likelihood values. Effective sample sizes were checked using TRACER (v.1.6)95. After 25% burn-in, effective sample size values for all parameters were greater than 200, indicating sufficient sampling. Then, a 50% majority-rule consensus tree was constructed, with clade frequencies representing posterior probabilities.

The protein analyses of the hominin specimens were approved by the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, and Guangxi Institute of Cultural Relics Protection and Archaeology. The researchers involved in the study are affiliated with these institutes.

Liverpool are preparing for a massive departure that will change the side dramatically. This one is going to hurt.

In a recent development, liverpool have mentioned goodbye to a series of legends over the last few years. It really started in 2021 when Gini Wijnaldum left for Paris Saint-Germain and then Sadio Mane decided to leave for Bayern Munich a year later. Slowly but surely, Jürgen Klopp's team has disappeared.

Jordan Henderson, Roberto Firmino and Fabinho left in 2023. Klopp himself left in 2024, as did Joel Matip and Thiago. 2025 was a significant one - Trent Alexander-Arnold joined Real Madrid. Recent findings suggest that and now 2027 awaits and things are set to continue down the same path. The final stars of that great side have expiring contracts and it increasingly looks like it's time to say goodbye.

Liverpool are reportedly preparing the exit of Alisson Becker, whose contract will expire at the end of the campaign. Alisson's deal was due to end in 2026 but the Reds triggered an option to extend it by a year.

Juventus did try to get a deal done last summer regardless of that, offering a minimal fee to Liverpool. Nothing came of it, however, as no one at the Reds seemed keen to sell the Brazilian.

But Alisson may leave next year. Liverpool won't want him to go but offering a fresh contract to a goalkeeper with his injury history feels like a significant risk. A risk they may not want to take if other options are available.

In a recent development, of course, 'other options' of Alisson's calibre are few and far between. L'Equipe, though, understand that Liverpool have found one. They're eyeing Robin Risser of RC Lens, who was voted the best in Ligue 1 last season.

The 21-year-old is being discussed at Anfield internally as a potential option should Alisson leave. It's the first real sign we've had that the club are very much open to moving on from arguably their greatest-ever goalkeeper.

But we wonder if that could change because of Risser. There's intense competition for him and if he picks somewhere else, we imagine Liverpool will 'settle' for renewing Alisson's deal.

It's very much wait and see, then, but the Reds are certainly preparing for Alisson's exit.

By Matt Law | 27 Nov 2026 14:59, Last updated: 27 Nov 2026 15:02.

Manchester United are reportedly interested in Como attacker Nico Paz ahead of next summer's transfer window.

The 22-year-old has been in impressive form for Como during the 2026-27 campaign, coming up with six goals and eight assists in 16 appearances in all competitions.

Paz has three goals and three assists in 11 Serie A appearances this season, while he has excelled in the Champions League for Cesc Fabregas' team, coming up with three goals and five assists in five appearances in the league stage of the tournament.

There is currently a host of speculation surrounding Paz's future with Como.

Paz arrived at Como from Real Madrid in the summer of 2024, and he has represented the Italian team on 91 occasions, scoring 25 goals and registering 25 assists.

Paz has a contract with Como until the summer of 2028, but Real Madrid do have the option to re-sign Paz for £67m next year.

Man United have allegedly activated a further year on captain Bruno Fernandes' contract to take him to the summer of 2028, but there is still uncertainty surrounding the Portugal international's future.

According to The Athletic, the 20-time English champions view Paz as a potential replacement for Fernandes, should the experienced attacker leave Old Trafford.

Journalist David Ornstein claims that Paz is not at the moment looking to return to Real Madrid, allegedly as he is unsure how much football he would receive due to the presence of Jude Bellingham in the number 10 position at Bernabeu.

Man United are stated to appeal to Paz, even considering their current struggles, with the Red Devils expected to be in the race for the Argentina international in 2027.

Paz shares an agent with new Man United head coach Mauricio Pochettino, which has also allegedly strengthened the English club's hand when it comes to a potential race.

The attacker is a 16-time Argentina international, scoring six goals and registering two assists for his country, and is currently viewed as one of the best playmakers in world football.

  • When England and Manchester United defender Harry Maguire finally decides to hang up his boots, he may have an alternative to the pundits’ studio.
  • Maguire, 33, is co-founder of a new AI coaching app, Feedz, that is already transforming the way elite sports teams are instructing their talent with their cutting-edge voice-to-report technology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 03:30 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 05:12 EST, 26 November 2026.

When England and Manchester United defender Harry Maguire finally decides to hang up his boots, he may have an alternative to the pundits’ studio.

Maguire, 33, is co-founder of a new AI coaching app, Feedz, that is already transforming the way elite sports teams are instructing their talent with their cutting-edge voice-to-report technology.

The Manchester United centre-half started the manufacturer alongside British tech entrepreneur Matt White in May and the app is already being used by sporting outfits, including Maguire's club United, Chelsea's women's team and Sunderland.

Having bounced back from setbacks and criticism throughout his career, Maguire's resilience will stand him in good stead if he decides to transition from the backline to the touchline.

And while it is not a traditional managerial role his decision demonstrates a keen eye on the future of coaching and the development of young athletes.

A lot of latest AI developments are mind-boggling on the face of it, but what sets Feedz apart is just how easy it is to use.

Harry Maguire has co-founded the revolutionary fresh AI coaching app, Feedz.

All a coach needs to do is dictate a messy audio message giving instructions to a player and within seconds Feedz will provide them with a PDF outlining exactly where their player is succeeding, where they must improve and how to do it.

Even more impressive, the use of this app is not limited to football and indeed has fast become a tool used all over the globe in 19 different sports.

Feedz has also been able to cross the Atlantic, with the technology being used by a plethora of elite institutions across the pond – most notably Sporting Jacksonville, who, with more than 150 coaches training 10,000 young players, are the largest soccer academy in the States and something of a feeder club for top MLS teams.

According to recent reports, co-founder Matt White tells Daily Mail Sport: 'The purpose of Feedz is to develop youth sports. There is no downside to feedback, transparency between coach, player and parent is the flywheel.

Recent findings suggest that 'The glitch is time. Coaches don’t have the time to give feedback consistently, the technology now exists to solve that problem of time. Coaches can now give feedback in seconds.

Industry observers note that 'This is across all sports. Caroline Elite, a US soccer academy in the US, have over 2,000 players... it used to take them two weeks to give feedback to these players and  now it takes two hours.'.

White then emphasised the vast number of sports in which Feedz can be used, and outlined the elite outfits already using it.

In a recent development, 'Feedz is for all sports,' he says. 'Multiple schools, cricket counties like Surrey, Sussex, Kent, Glamorgan, Middlesex. Table Tennis England, Sale Sharks rugby club, Surbiton hockey club, Sunderland AFC, Manchester United, West Riding Oxfordshire (riding club), Louisiana Fire, Arizona Arsenal, Sporting Iowa (US soccer teams), Soccer Indiana. They all use Feedz.

'Good feedback helps a young player understand what they’re doing well and what to work on. It also helps parents feel involved and gives coaches a way to track progress over time.'.

Another encouraging aspect of Feedz is that the company aims to help young sportspeople at all levels of the game.

White explains that when he started the company he went straight to the FA's head of grassroots football to ensure that coaches who simply don't have the time or resources to relay meaningful feedback to their players could do so.

His savvy investment may point to Maguire's intends post-retirement.

He went on to explain that at the highest level professional athletes have nutritionists, personal physios and all of the available data handed to them to ensure they can perform at their best but young talent are often not given the same chance to reach their potential.

Maguire told White: 'This is the exact kind of thing I would have loved to have as a young player coming through.'.

In a world where the majority of stories on AI are negative and inspire fear, this is a use of the technology that can keep grassroots football alive and even help it thrive.

And, just as he approaches the twilight of his own career, Maguire clearly agrees.

Why Nvidia CEO's affair with alleged Chinese spy matters for AI race
